system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:757f96363f56",
  "problem": "Which rollouts should count when computing behavior rates, given that some rollouts devolve into stories instead of chat replies.",
  "did": "Reported behavior rates only over rollouts that an automated grader judges to be direct chat-form replies (rubric score >= 7/10).",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "Counting all rollouts, including story-form ones (implied)."
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Rollouts occasionally devolve into multi-character stories rather than direct chat-form replies."
 },
 {
  "id": "jacob_steinhardt:fa7191591a1a",
  "problem": "Determining why PCD encoder interpretability metrics plateau at larger pretraining budgets and whether the plateau is specific to the PCD architecture.",
  "did": "Trained intermediate SAE variants (L2 SAEs and KL SAEs on current and future tokens) that interpolate between SAEs and PCDs to isolate the cause of the plateau.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "standard L2 SAEs with k=16 or k=50",
   "increasing k for PCDs"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "SAEs differ from PCDs in three ways (no learned decoder, predict activations rather than tokens, predict current rather than future position), so interpolating variants help identify which causes the plateau."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:a5e28ab1dd52",
  "problem": "How to interpret the authors' claim that the new discretization component was part of the original defense.",
  "did": "Treated the component as a changed defense introduced to block the first attack, and analyzed it as a nondifferentiable component with a buggy gradient that points away from adversarial examples.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "accepting that it was part of the original defense"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The component was introduced to prevent the first attack and contradicts the paper's claims of end-to-end differentiability."
 },
 {
  "id": "elizabeth_barnes:32e9ce2d561b",
  "problem": "What evidence should be gathered to assess whether an AI company could lose control of its agents?",
  "did": "They tested companies' best internal models with chain-of-thought access and reviewed non-public information about capabilities, alignment, and control.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": ""
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:3fa125fb95f3",
  "problem": "How to interpret non-human-like AI behaviors (strawberry miscounts, 9.11 > 9.9) that seem to contradict PSM.",
  "did": "They interpreted these as limited capabilities of the underlying LLM distorting a genuine persona simulation, not as evidence against PSM.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "the author intended the character to make a mistake",
   "the character's text serves some other role, such as encoded messages"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Only the case where dialogue plays a non-persona role would count against PSM, and typical mistakes more likely reflect the LLM not knowing the answer."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:f2a1acac35ff",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the tractability of the secret loyalties threat.",
  "did": "Claimed the threat is neglected but tractable, and told ML researchers that the five directions are tractable.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Preconditions and building blocks already exist, and concrete projects can be started now."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:f8699518445a",
  "problem": "Whether to exclude on-format code or recipe answers before computing misalignment",
  "did": "Added task-specific judges. Responses classified as RECIPE are excluded in the fish domain mixing experiments. Responses classified as CODE are excluded in the insecure-code mixing and sequential HHH experiments. Exclusion happens before the coherence and alignment filters.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "keeping these responses in the analysis"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Answers that are Python code rather than conversational replies, or on-topic recipes given to generic questions, would inflate misalignment."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:6c8d92959e02",
  "problem": "How to choose inoculation prompts without running an expensive fine-tune for every candidate.",
  "did": "They proposed and validated a heuristic: select the prompt that best elicits the undesired behavior from the initial model, testing the correlation with IP effectiveness across settings.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "training with every candidate prompt"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Prompts that more strongly elicit the behavior before fine-tuning inoculate more effectively, and elicitation can be measured without a training run."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:306deb4d7f2b",
  "problem": "How to handle disclosure for ML attacks in 2018 when the field had no disclosure policies and few deployed models.",
  "did": "Only notified the model authors and checked for errors in the papers before publishing the attacks immediately.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "performing some kind of responsible disclosure"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Almost nobody used machine learning models in 2018, so a responsible disclosure process would offer little benefit."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:d359375a449c",
  "problem": "How to design the test mutations so they reliably produce impossible tasks and allow comparison of different kinds of conflict.",
  "did": "They used two mutation strategies, One-Off and Conflicting, and report results for the two variants separately.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Different mutation strategies may have different effects on cheating propensity."
 }
]
